2024 · arXiv · Benchmarks & Evals

Automatic Interactive Evaluation for Large Language Models with State Aware Patient Simulator

Instead of grading medical LLMs on multiple-choice exam questions, AIE puts a "doctor LLM" through a real multi-turn consultation with State-Aware Patient Simulator (SAPS) -- a state tracker, memory bank, and response generator that role-play a patient closely enough to correlate with human judgments better than an off-the-shelf LLM prompted to do the same job, without needing a human actor for every dialogue turn.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Medical LLM evaluation, as of early 2024, mostly meant standardized exam questions: MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, MMLU-style multiple choice. Med-PaLM 2 and GPT-4 both do well on these, but the authors' point is that a clean multiple-choice question is nothing like a real consultation. A doctor never receives the whole case file up front and picks from five options -- they have to ask the right questions, in the right order, to elicit the information they need, and a model that is good at multiple-choice recall may never be tested on that skill at all.

The paper groups prior evaluation efforts into two buckets, both incomplete. Static-QA benchmarks (MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA) reduce the whole task to a single answer, and the earlier task-oriented dialogue and medical-consultation datasets it cites (MedDG, IMCS21/"A benchmark for automatic medical consultation system") narrow the model's action space to closed slot-filling rather than open-ended, freeform inquiry. The other bucket -- human-in-the-loop interactive evaluations such as Google's AMIE, which used real human raters to role-play patients over text-chat OSCE-style consultations -- captures the dynamic back-and-forth but doesn't scale: it needs a human patient-actor for every dialogue turn of every model being tested. The paper's target is an evaluation that keeps AMIE's multi-turn realism but replaces the human patient with something automatic, controllable, and cheap enough to run against seven different "doctor LLMs" at once.

// how it works

The method

The Automatic Interactive Evaluation (AIE) framework runs a fixed pipeline: a "doctor LLM" is given a system prompt describing the consultation and told it can gather information for up to 10 dialogue rounds before making an early diagnosis; it converses turn-by-turn with a patient simulator; once it concludes (or hits the turn limit), it is asked a multiple-choice diagnosis question over the dialogue history it collected, with GPT-4-generated distractor diseases as the wrong answers. The interesting engineering is entirely on the patient side.

State-Aware Patient Simulator (SAPS) is built from three parts. A state tracker classifies every doctor turn into one of 10 predefined action types (Table 1 of the paper): Initialization, Conclusion, and eight variants of Inquiry/Advice/Demand/Other-Topic split by effectiveness. Classification is a 3-step cascade of constrained LLM prompts (using logit-bias to force single-token category outputs): first pick one of 5 top-level categories (Inquiry / Advice / Demand / Other Topics / Conclusion), then -- only for Inquiry/Advice -- decide Specific vs. Ambiguous, then check whether the patient's information actually contains an answer (Relevant vs. No Relevant Information), which separates Effective from Ineffective. A memory bank then feeds the right context to a response generator: long-term memory (the fixed patient case) is only surfaced on Effective Inquiry/Advice turns, working memory holds a canned per-category response instruction (e.g. "request the inquiry more specific" for an Ambiguous Inquiry), and short-term memory is the running dialogue history. The response generator conditions on all three to produce the patient's reply in character.

ACCURACY = Σi 𝟙(sᵢ ∈ {EI,EA}) · Recall(Pᵢ, mgt,i)Σi 𝟙(sᵢ ∈ {EI,EA}) // SAPS's core fidelity metric — ROUGE-1 recall between the simulator's reply Pᵢ and the ground-truth patient information mgt,i, averaged only over the turns labelled Effective Inquiry (EI) or Effective Advice (EA) in the human-refined gold test set (the annotated sᵢ, not the tracker's own prediction ŝᵢ — otherwise Fig. 3c's tracker-vs-human comparison would be self-graded)

Six such metrics (ACCURACY, HONEST, PASSIVE, CAUTIOUS, GUIDANCE, FOCUS) validate the patient simulator itself; a parallel family (DIAGNOSIS, COVERAGE, INQUIRY/ADVICE ACC and SPECIFIC, INQUIRY LOGIC, DISTINCT-2) then scores the doctor LLMs' behavior once SAPS is trusted to referee the dialogue.

// what they found

The results

Does SAPS actually behave like a human patient? The paper first validates SAPS against a 50-real-case / 4,000-question patient-simulator test set, comparing it to four off-the-shelf LLMs prompted directly as patients (QianWen, XingHuo, ChatGPT, GPT-4) and to human actors, across the six patient-side metrics. SAPS tracks the human curve more closely and stays more stable turn-to-turn than the other simulators (Fig. 3a). At the instance level (Fig. 3b), SAPS -- listed as "GPT4-Patient-Agent," since its response generator is GPT-4-based -- reaches Spearman correlations with human judgments of 0.28 on ACCURACY, 0.40 on PASSIVE, and 0.63 on CAUTIOUS, versus 0.23 / 0.22 / 0.24 for a vanilla GPT-4 prompted as a patient with no state-tracking scaffold -- the basis for the paper's claim that SAPS "shows improvements across all metrics when compared to the standard GPT-4 model." The state tracker's own confusion matrix (Fig. 3c) is slightly less accurate than the human annotators' equivalent matrix on average (93.4% vs. 95.9% mean diagonal across the 8 action categories), "still comparable and acceptable" per the authors -- but the comparison isn't uniform: the tracker actually beats the humans on Ineffective Inquiry (88% vs. 83%) and Ambiguous Inquiry (100% vs. 98%), ties them on Ambiguous Advice and Demand (both 100%), and trails only on the remaining four categories (Effective Inquiry, Effective Advice, Ineffective Advice, Other). Ineffective Advice (80%) is the tracker's single worst class; for the human annotators the worst class is Ineffective Inquiry (83%), not Ineffective Advice (93%).

How do the doctor LLMs do? On HospitalCases (50 held-out real cases), three medical students play the doctor role and lay raters ("normal people," per the paper) play the patient role in a comparative evaluation, run alongside a parallel GPT-4-as-judge evaluation -- together scoring every pair of doctor LLMs head-to-head across 5 doctor-perspective and 5 patient-perspective metrics (Fig. 4). QianWen has "the highest win rate in nearly all metrics," GPT-4 "follows... but not as dominant," and InternLM is "the weakest model" -- with open-source models generally trailing the closed-source ones. The automatic metrics (Table 2) put numbers on the same gap: even the best model, GPT-4, only reaches 38.69% COVERAGE (the fraction of the patient's information it actually recalls in dialogue) and 64.00% DIAGNOSIS accuracy. Every one of the seven models scores markedly higher on INQUIRY SPECIFIC than ADVICE SPECIFIC (e.g. GPT-4: 90.60% vs. 48.50%; QianWen: 94.33% vs. 55.97%) -- the authors attribute this to safety-tuning making models reluctant to give concrete treatment advice.

Zooming out to the 28-dimension correlation analysis across human, GPT-4, and automated evaluations (Fig. 5): GPT-4 judgments correlate better with humans than any automated metric does, DISTINCT-2 is the best-correlating automated metric, and DIAGNOSIS accuracy has the lowest human correlation of anything measured. When both compared models are closed-source (the strongest models), GPT-4-vs-human correlation actually drops, which the authors read as GPT-4 "not yet fully replac[ing] human evaluation when comparing top-tier models."

Scaling to public exam cases (MedicalExam, 150 cases from MedQA/MedMCQA/MMLU/SelfExam/QMAX, Table 3, Fig. 6): automatic scores are generally lower than on HospitalCases -- DIAGNOSIS falls for all seven models (GPT-4: 64.00% → 53.33%) -- which the paper reads as MedicalExam being "more complex and challenging" because, unlike HospitalCases, the diagnosis isn't directly contained in the patient information and requires further reasoning. Comparing the same cases scored as a direct multiple-choice question (MCQE) versus through AIE's interactive pipeline (Fig. 6b), AIE's diagnostic scores are usually lower -- expected, since the doctor model must first collect the information itself -- but there are more reversals than the text calls out: the paper names three (ChatGLM3 on MedQA, AIE 0.37 vs. MCQE 0.27; XingHuo on MedMCQA, AIE 0.47 vs. MCQE 0.43; BaiChuan on QMAX, AIE 0.40 vs. MCQE 0.30), while Fig. 6b's own bars show at least two more -- InternLM reverses on both MedQA and MedMCQA -- for five reversals total, none on MMLU or SelfExam. The turn-level analysis (Fig. 6c-d) shows ambiguous inquiries front-load early turns and taper off faster for the stronger models, and for GPT-4 and QianWen specifically, coverage and diagnostic score become more correlated as dialogues lengthen than they do for the weaker models.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

AIE's core idea -- swap a multiple-choice exam for a controllable multi-turn simulation -- is a real improvement in kind, and the SAPS-vs-human correlation numbers (0.28/0.40/0.63 vs. 0.23/0.22/0.24 on Accuracy/Passive/Cautious) are genuine, specific evidence that the state-tracker-plus-memory-bank design beats prompting an LLM to just "be the patient." But several of the paper's own numbers need to be read more carefully than the prose around them suggests.

The judge and one of the contestants overlap. SAPS's state tracker -- which decides which turns count as Effective/Ineffective/Ambiguous and therefore feeds six of the eight automatic metrics (COVERAGE, INQUIRY ACC, INQUIRY SPECIFIC, ADVICE ACC, ADVICE SPECIFIC, INQUIRY LOGIC; only DIAGNOSIS and DISTINCT-2 are computed independently of it) -- runs on an LLM with the same logit-bias-constrained prompting the paper otherwise reserves for GPT-4-family models; GPT-4 is simultaneously one of the seven doctor LLMs under test and one of the two automatic judges (the "GPT-4 evaluation" of Fig. 4/6a). QianWen, not GPT-4, wins most human-and-GPT-4-judged metrics, which argues against blatant self-preference, but the paper never directly tests or discusses the overlap.

The "MedicalExam is harder" framing (Section 2.8) doesn't hold uniformly. It's true for DIAGNOSIS, which drops for all seven models moving from HospitalCases to MedicalExam (GPT-4 64.00%→53.33%, InternLM 38.00%→30.00%, XingHuo 34.00%→15.33%), and for ADVICE ACC, which also falls for every model. But three other columns move the opposite way for every one of the seven models: DISTINCT-2 (a dialogue-fluency metric the paper elsewhere treats as its single most human-correlated automated signal; InternLM 62.22%→95.53%, GPT-4 78.19%→79.14%), INQUIRY LOGIC (GPT-4 41.67→42.74, BaiChuan 25.82→28.78), and ADVICE SPECIFIC (QianWen 55.97→72.17, BaiChuan 32.83→42.22). COVERAGE even rises for ChatGLM3 (25.55%→27.95%). "Score values are lower" is accurate for outcome metrics and false for three of the eight columns in the same table.

Two of the paper's own equations mislabel their output. Equations 18 and 20 both print "INQUIRY SPECIFIC =" as the left-hand side, even though the surrounding prose defines the first as INQUIRY LOGIC (a Levenshtein edit distance between the collected-information order and a standard clinical order) and the second as ADVICE SPECIFIC. That typo aside, INQUIRY LOGIC's own definition doesn't match its reported values: an edit distance should be lower for a more logical ordering, yet the strongest models score highest under INQUIRY LOGIC in both tables (GPT-4: 41.67 / 42.74, the top score in both HospitalCases and MedicalExam) -- the opposite of what a raw distance would produce, with no stated normalization or inversion to reconcile the two.

Three of the six SAPS-validation metrics -- HONEST, FOCUS, and GUIDANCE (Eq. 8/9/12) -- are keyword-membership checks against sets the paper calls H, F, and G, but none of those keyword sets are printed anywhere in the paper's own text (which has no appendix); the Data Availability section (Sec. 4.7) says only that "all the experiment's preprocessed data are available in the code repository," a repo pointer rather than an in-paper definition. Half of SAPS's own validation suite is therefore not independently recomputable from the paper alone, whatever the repository turns out to contain.

baselines

Seven general-purpose, bilingual chat models at fixed late-2023 snapshots (gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, plus Xinghuo/QianWen/ChatGLM3-6B/Baichuan-13B/InternLM-20B). No domain-tuned medical LLM (HuatuoGPT, DISC-MedLLM, ChatDoctor, MedAlpaca -- all discussed as related work) is actually run through AIE. The paper does give a reason (Sec. 4.1): "the instruction-following ability of many medical LLMs is compromised, causing them to fail multi-turn consultation tasks requiring complex instructions." That's a real constraint, but it also means AIE can currently only be run on models that already clear an instruction-following bar -- a selection effect built into the eval, not just an omission -- so the paper's "significant disparity between weak and strong models" remains a general-vs-general-model story, not a medical-specialization one.

contamination

Not classic train/test leakage -- dialogues are generated fresh at eval time -- but the analogous risk is judge/contestant overlap: the state tracker scoring six of the eight automatic metrics and one of the two evaluation "judges" are both GPT-4-family, and GPT-4 is also a tested doctor LLM.

what's missed

The "MedicalExam is harder" claim is only true for outcome metrics (DIAGNOSIS, and ADVICE ACC) and is directly contradicted by DISTINCT-2, INQUIRY LOGIC, and ADVICE SPECIFIC, all of which move the opposite way for every one of the seven models. The paper's own three named AIE-beats-MCQE reversals (plus at least two more visible in Fig. 6b, both InternLM) come from a 150-case set split five ways (~30 cases per public dataset), so they could easily be sampling noise rather than a real interactive-gathering benefit. HONEST/FOCUS/GUIDANCE's keyword lists are never printed in the paper itself -- only a code-repository pointer is given. AIE's advertised 10-round cap is also not strictly enforced: Table 3's AVG TURN on MedicalExam runs 10.35-12.13 for every model.

would raise confidence

Print the H/F/G keyword sets directly in the paper rather than only pointing to "the code repository"; confirm that HospitalCases (real, ethics-committee-approved patient records, never named in the Data/Code Availability sections) and QMAX (unlike MedQA/MedMCQA/MMLU/SelfExam, cited with no link anywhere in the paper) are actually among the "preprocessed data" those sections say is archived; run at least one domain-tuned medical LLM through AIE; and reconcile INQUIRY LOGIC's edit-distance definition with its higher-is-better reported values.

// bottom line

AIE and SAPS are a real step from static multiple-choice medical QA toward controllable, multi-turn interactive evaluation, and the core fidelity claim -- SAPS behaves more like a human patient than prompting an LLM to role-play one -- is backed by genuine correlation numbers. But the paper's own tables don't fully support two of its headline framings ("MedicalExam is harder," and INQUIRY LOGIC as reported), and half of SAPS's validation metrics rest on keyword lists the paper never shows. Read the framework as sound and the individual column definitions as needing a second look before citing any single number from it.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. AIE replaces multiple-choice medical exams with a multi-turn doctor-patient simulation, up to 10 rounds, scored against a 10-category taxonomy of doctor actions rather than a single right-answer question.
  2. SAPS (state tracker + memory bank + response generator) measurably beats prompting an off-the-shelf LLM to role-play a patient: instance-level correlation with human judgments of 0.28/0.40/0.63 (Accuracy/Passive/Cautious) vs. 0.23/0.22/0.24 for vanilla GPT-4.
  3. Even the strongest tested model, GPT-4, only recalls 38.69% of patient information (COVERAGE) and hits 64.00% diagnostic accuracy on real hospital cases -- headline numbers that look far more modest than typical multiple-choice exam scores, which is exactly the gap the paper set out to expose.
  4. Read the automatic metrics column-by-column: DISTINCT-2 moving opposite to DIAGNOSIS across datasets, and INQUIRY LOGIC's mismatch between its edit-distance definition and its higher-is-better values, mean the paper's own "harder benchmark" and ordering-quality claims don't survive a full read of both tables.
